# 142 · An ASCII fast path for the constant-pool encoder proved equal to the previous version at bound eight

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: equivalent on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | refactor, behaviour change not intended | [`ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/classfile/ModifiedUtf8.java) | [B9: Regression verification](../../lib/README.md) |

> The class-file writer encodes every string constant into modified UTF-8 with `ModifiedUtf8#encodeInto`, which tests each `char` for the one-, two- or three-byte form. Most constants are ASCII, so a developer adds a fast path: a leading run of one-byte characters, recognised by `(char) (c - 1) < 0x7f`, is copied without the general test, and the general loop takes over at the first character that is not. The regression proof against the previous version, which JBMC could not finish at the default bound of eight characters in 2.8 GB, is done by the tool's own checker in 7 s and 76 MB: once the search has grown past a few hundred paths, the paths through the loops are merged at their join points, so the proof explores 733 paths where there are 11643, and at a bound of twelve characters it is done in 83 s where the unmerged search exhausted its budget of 200000 paths without a verdict.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [class-files](../README.md#tag-class-files), [text-encoding](../README.md#tag-text-encoding), [array-utilities](../README.md#tag-array-utilities), [own-checker](../README.md#tag-own-checker)

## The change

Before the general loop, copy the leading run of one-byte characters: while `(char) (chars[i] - 1) < 0x7f`, which is U+0001 to U+007F, write `(byte) chars[i]` and move on; the general loop then starts at `i` instead of 0. The encoder's tests pass: `abc` encodes to its ASCII bytes, and `a\u0000字` to six bytes, NUL as two and the CJK character as three.


```java
public static int encodeInto(char[] chars, byte[] out) {
    int k = 0;
    int i = 0;
    // Most constants are ASCII: copy the leading run of one-byte characters without the general test.
    while (i < chars.length && (char) (chars[i] - 1) < 0x7f) {
        out[k++] = (byte) chars[i++];
    }
    for (; i < chars.length; i++) {
        char c = chars[i];
        if (c >= 0x0001 && c <= 0x007f) {
            out[k++] = (byte) c;
        } else if (c <= 0x07ff) {
```

## What the verifier found

For every input, the new code returns what the old code returned, or throws what it threw.

This is a proof over the whole domain (chars: char[] of length ≤ 8 × out: byte[] of length ≤ 8), not a sample. The tool's own checker ran the harness symbolically, path by path, with its bundled SAT solver deciding at each branch which sides are feasible, and no feasible path reaches the assertion: no input exists on which they differ.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

A fast path is a second copy of a rule, and the two copies drift: the test that decides which characters it takes has to be exactly the one the general loop's first branch makes, on the `char` arithmetic of the JVM, where `c - 1` is an `int` and the cast back to `char` wraps U+0000 to U+FFFF. A string constant encoded wrongly is a class file the virtual machine rejects (`ClassFormatError`) or a string with the wrong characters in it, for every class the writer produces with that constant. The tests cover the characters somebody thought of.

## Why the verdict is right

The regression proof asks whether the new `encodeInto` returns what the previous one returned, writes what it wrote into `out`, or throws what it threw, on every `chars` and `out` of up to eight elements. The harness copies both arrays, calls each version on its copy, and compares the results and the copies element by element. The tool's own checker runs it with the arrays as objects of a symbolic length and a cell per index. Every branch inside the loops is feasible for some input, so the paths through eight iterations of three-way branching are thousands; once 512 paths have been explored each on its own, the checker merges the paths that reach the same instruction of the same calls, a loop header or the instruction after an `if`, into one path whose state is a choice by the condition of each, and keeps the models of the paths merged, so a branch each of whose sides some model takes costs no solver call. The proof explores 733 paths, 219 of them merged into another, with 1885 solver calls, in 7 s and 76 MB; the same harness unmerged takes 11643 paths and 46063 calls in 5.6 s, and at a bound of twelve characters the merged search is done in 83 s where the unmerged one exhausts 200000 paths with no verdict. JBMC, given the harness at the bound of eight, ran out of memory at 2.8 GB in 15 s on this machine, and proved the versions equal only up to four characters, in 275 s.

## What to do

None needed. The example is a proof of a refactoring that holds: the fast path's test is the general loop's first branch, and the bound of eight (or twelve) characters covers every way the run of one-byte characters can end, including a buffer too short for the encoding, which both versions leave the same way.

## Notes

- This proof waited from 1 to 4 November 2026 in `examples/apps/mica/pending` for a machine with more memory: JBMC at `--max-array-length 8 --unwind 16` ran out of memory at 2.8 GB in 15 s (and at 5.7 GB before a limit was set), and at bounds 2, 3 and 4 proved the versions equal in 31, 94 and 275 s. The tool's own checker proves it at the default bound in 7 s and 76 MB, and at twelve characters in 83 s and 155 MB, so the pending proof became this example and example 143.
- Path merging in the tool's own checker is what this example exercises: without it the checker explores 11643 paths with 46063 solver calls in 5.6 s at the bound of eight, and at a bound of twelve exhausts its budget of 200000 paths after 128 s with no verdict. Merged after the first 512 paths, the search is 733 paths at eight and 868 at twelve; merged from the start it is 237 and 369. The time at eight does not fall, because the solver's work moves: the comparisons of the output cells at the end of the harness, one per element of each version's copy, are each a proof over the merged formula, and the sixteen of them take most of the 7 s. At sixteen the search merged from the start had 488 paths and 678 solver calls after four minutes and no verdict, each call over a formula of 163000 variables, where the unmerged search had spent its path budget after 145 s; the bound the proof scales to on this machine is twelve. The first 512 paths are left unmerged because a small search is cheaper that way: a solver call about one concrete path is cheap, one about a disjunction of paths is not, and the 64-bit arithmetic of examples 131, 134 and 139 took two to three times as long merged from the start.
- The bound applies to `chars` and `out` alike, so an input whose encoding needs more bytes than `out` holds overflows the buffer in both versions and is compared up to that exception; eight three-byte characters need 24 bytes and are never encoded to the end. A difference that only shows past the eighth byte written would not be seen. Example 143's difference shows in the first byte.
- The fast path's test `(char) (chars[i] - 1) < 0x7f` is one comparison for the two the general loop makes (`c >= 0x0001 && c <= 0x007f`): the subtraction wraps U+0000 to U+FFFF, which fails the test, as it should, since U+0000 takes the two-byte form. The proof covers the wrap, since `chars` has every value in its cells.
- The encoder's properties in `properties.contract` (examples 044, 048 and 055) hold of both versions; they say how many bytes are written and what the first byte of each character is, not that the new version writes what the old one wrote. The regression proof is a different statement, which the properties do not imply either way: example 143 is a fast path the properties allow and the regression proof refutes.
- Gap scan (step 1a of `llm-dlc/loops/sound-verdicts.md`, 5 November 2026, JDK 25.0.4.1, from the bytecode, nothing proved): the tool's own checker meets no gap in the 1 method the proof reaches in either version, so strict mode does not move this verdict.

## Evidence

How the verdict was reached: jvmcontract's own checker (CaDiCaL): 1 properties proved over chars: char[] of length ≤ 8 × out: byte[] of length ≤ 8 in 6.4 s; loops unwound 16 times with unwinding assertions.

This result was recorded before runs fingerprinted their inputs, so whether it still matches the current patch and sources is not known.

<details><summary>The statement the prover checked (generated harness)</summary>

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts that two versions of a method agree. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class EquivalenceHarness {
    public static void check(char[] chars, byte[] out) {
        char[] chars_before = java.util.Arrays.copyOf(chars, chars.length); // the version before writes into its own copy
        byte[] out_before = java.util.Arrays.copyOf(out, out.length); // the version before writes into its own copy
        int a = 0;
        int ea = 0;
        try { a = before.net.terminalvalue.mica.classfile.ModifiedUtf8.encodeInto(chars_before, out_before); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { ea = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { ea = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { ea = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { ea = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { ea = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { ea = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { ea = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { ea = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { ea = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { ea = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { ea = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { ea = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { ea = 15; }
        int b = 0;
        int eb = 0;
        try { b = net.terminalvalue.mica.classfile.ModifiedUtf8.encodeInto(chars, out); } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { eb = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { eb = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { eb = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { eb = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { eb = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { eb = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { eb = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { eb = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { eb = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { eb = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { eb = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { eb = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { eb = 15; }
        assert ea == eb && (ea != 0 || a == b) && java.util.Arrays.equals(chars, chars_before) && java.util.Arrays.equals(out, out_before);
    }
}
```
